vignette:
He is a 42-year-old South Eastern Asian man who makes his living as a farmer, and when he speaks about his life he does so in the rhythm of seasons. He remembers years by harvests, droughts, and floods, and he remembers the year his son nearly died as the year everything in his body stopped trusting the world.

Before that, his days are steady and physical. He wakes before sunrise, walks the fields while the air is still cool, checks the irrigation channels, and returns home with mud on his calves and the smell of wet earth on his clothes. He is not a man who talks much about feelings. He shows love by working, by repairing what is broken, by bringing food home. His wife handles much of the household, and together they raise their children with the ordinary worries of any family. Their youngest son is lively, always following him into the yard, always asking to help.

The illness begins like something small. His son develops a fever that does not break. At first he tells himself children get sick and recover. But over the next day the boy becomes limp and glassy-eyed, too weak to sit up, then begins struggling to breathe. He can still picture the way his son’s skin looks that night, hot and dull at once, and the sound his wife makes when she realizes this is no ordinary fever. He carries the child to a vehicle with the frantic care of someone holding both something precious and something fragile beyond belief. On the drive to the hospital, he keeps touching the boy’s chest to make sure it is still rising.

The hospital is all fluorescent light, disinfectant, metal rails, and waiting. There are words from doctors that come too quickly, terms he does not fully understand, urgent faces, needles, oxygen, signatures. His son is moved into intensive care. Machines begin speaking in beeps and alarms. He stands beside the bed feeling useless, watching strangers do everything that matters. The helplessness is what he returns to most often now. He cannot plow a field or mend a pump or bargain at market his way out of that moment. He can only watch his child disappear under wires and tubes.

For several days he barely leaves the hospital. He dozes upright in a plastic chair, jerking awake every time a monitor changes tone. When nurses rush into the room once, his whole body turns cold. Even now he remembers that instant as if time split open: his wife crying, a doctor calling instructions, his son’s small body looking impossibly still. He is certain, in that moment, that he is about to lose him. He later says that something in him never fully comes back from those hours.

His son survives, but after discharge life does not return to what it was before. Everyone around him treats the recovery as a blessing and a closure. He also knows it is a blessing, and this makes him feel ashamed of how frightened and changed he remains. At home he begins checking on the boy repeatedly through the night, placing a hand near his mouth to feel breath, sometimes waking him just to hear him answer. If the child sleeps too deeply, panic rises so fast he feels dizzy. Minor coughs, low fevers, even naps that last too long can send him into a state of alarm. He keeps imagining ambulances, hospital corridors, funerals.

Back in the fields, he is no longer settled by routine. The whine of the water pump sometimes blends in his mind with the hospital machines, and he feels his chest tighten. If his phone rings while he is far from the house, he is immediately certain something terrible has happened. He leaves work half-done to race home. During planting season, when concentration matters, he finds himself staring at the soil without knowing what he has just done. He misplaces tools, forgets instructions, and has to redo tasks he once completed automatically. He is embarrassed when neighbors notice. He says he has become a man with one ear always turned toward danger.

At night he sleeps lightly or not at all. He dreams of hospital monitors going silent, of arriving too late, of his son calling for him from behind a closed door. He wakes sweating, heart pounding, sometimes already on his feet before he fully knows where he is. His wife tells him he startles at small sounds now—the slam of a gate, a coughing fit from another room, thunder during the rainy season. He has become more irritable with everyone, then immediately guilty. He snaps at his older children for making noise, then sits alone afterward, hating himself for it.

He avoids passing the hospital if he can. He avoids talking about the worst night, especially with relatives who say, “It is over now.” Yet he lives as though it is not over. The world feels thin to him, too easily torn. He says that before, he believed hard work could protect a family from most things. Now, even on a clear morning, while standing in his own field with the sun coming up and his son laughing somewhere behind him, part of him is braced for catastrophe. He wants to be present in the life that was spared, but fear keeps pulling him back to that room of bright lights and machines, where he learned how quickly love can turn into terror.
